title: Restraint, seclusion and post-incident care
blurb: Apply NICE NG10 and the MHA Code to safe manual restraint, seclusion reviews, long-term segregation and post-incident debrief.
question: Kwame, 30, detained under section 3, punches a nurse and is held by three staff. He is taken to the floor face down and is shouting that he cannot breathe. What should the nurse leading the restraint do?

teach.body: The MHA Code defines restrictive interventions as deliberate acts that restrict a patient's movement, liberty or freedom to act, to take immediate control of a dangerous situation and end or reduce the danger. They must be proportionate, the least restrictive option and used for no longer than necessary, never to punish. In plain English: you hold, sedate or separate someone only to stop serious harm, as gently and briefly as you can.
teach.cite: MHA Code of Practice 2015, 26.36-26.37; NICE NG10 1.4.5-1.4.7

rows.label: Position
values: Avoid the floor; supine if needed

rows.label: Face
values: Hand or cloth over the face

teach.caption: COP15 26.70: no planned or intentional prone restraint on any surface unless there are cogent reasons.

children.label: Seclusion may be used
children.sub: Last resort, designated room, Code safeguards

teach.caption: Seclusion is never a punishment, a threat, a response to staff shortage or part of a treatment programme (26.107).
COP15 26.103 and 26.150-26.155. Calling it 'therapeutic isolation' does not change what it is (26.104).

teach.body: Charge Nurse Ellis is leading. 'Cannot breathe' is a red flag. She tells the team to release any pressure on Kwame's back and to roll him onto his side then his back, keeps his head and neck supported and checks his airway, breathing and colour while speaking calmly to him. As the hold continues, she asks for the doctor to consider rapid tranquillisation or seclusion rather than a prolonged hold. Afterwards she leads an immediate debrief with a doctor and records the use of force.

teach.text: Seclusion is not decided by the room or the label. If a patient is confined alone and prevented from leaving, even at their own request, it IS seclusion and all the Code safeguards apply. And the 15-minute written record in seclusion is not the same as the 2-hourly nursing review.

steps.sub: Nurse and doctor: physical harm, risks, emotional impact (1.4.55)

steps.label: Patient's voice
steps.sub: Discuss with staff, advocate or carer; write their view in notes (1.4.58)

steps.label: Record
steps.sub: Use of Force Act record; care plan updated

items: Avoid the floor; if needed use supine, and prone as briefly as possible with no pressure on neck, chest or abdomen.
One lead protects the head, neck and airway and monitors vital signs throughout.
Seclusion only for detained patients; an informal patient secluded in an emergency needs an immediate MHA assessment.
Seclusion: 15-minute records, 1-hour medical review, 2-hourly two-nurse reviews, 4-hourly medical reviews.
Immediate debrief with a nurse and a doctor after every restrictive intervention.

summary: You can now lead or support a safe manual restraint that protects airway, breathing and circulation, and apply the Code's seclusion and long-term segregation safeguards. You can also explain who may be secluded and how post-incident debrief and review should follow.

A.q: If a patient has to be taken to the floor during manual restraint, which position does NICE NG10 prefer?
options: Prone (face down)
Supine (face up)
Kneeling against a wall
Seated on a chair
A.why: NG10 1.4.24: avoid taking the person to the floor; if necessary use the supine position if possible, and prone for as short a time as possible.

whyNot.0: Prone is to be used for as short a time as possible and avoided unless cogent reasons exist (COP15 26.70).
whyNot.2: Kneeling against a wall is not a recognised safe floor position in NG10.
whyNot.3: A seated hold is not a floor position and is not the NG10 preference.

A.q: How often must the observing staff member make a written record of a secluded patient's condition under the MHA Code?
options: At least every hour
At least every 2 hours
At least every 15 minutes
At least every 4 hours
A.why: COP15 26.123: a record of the patient's behaviour should be made at least every 15 minutes.

whyNot.0: Hourly records apply to long-term segregation, not seclusion.
whyNot.1: Two-hourly is the interval for nursing reviews by two nurses.
whyNot.3: Four-hourly is the interval for medical reviews until the first MDT review.

A.q: Under NICE NG10, who should be included in the immediate post-incident debrief after a restraint?
options: A nurse and a doctor
The ward manager and police
The patient's nearest relative
Two members of the security team
A.why: NG10 1.4.55: conduct an immediate post-incident debrief including a nurse and a doctor once risks are contained.

whyNot.1: Police are not part of the clinical debrief NG10 describes.
whyNot.2: Carers are informed with the patient's agreement, but the debrief itself involves a nurse and doctor.
whyNot.3: Security staff are not the clinicians NG10 specifies.

B.q: Hannah, 36, an informal patient, suddenly attacks another patient and, as a last resort, is placed in seclusion. What must happen next?
options: Continue seclusion and review it at the 8-hour mark
Discharge her from the ward for breaching rules
Ask her to sign a consent form for the seclusion
Arrange an immediate Mental Health Act assessment
B.why: COP15 26.106 and NG10 1.4.46: seclusion is for detained patients; if an informal patient is secluded in an emergency, arrange an MHA assessment immediately.

whyNot.0: Waiting 8 hours leaves an informal patient confined without legal authority.
whyNot.1: Discharge does not address the risk or her care needs.
whyNot.2: Consent does not change the legal position; agreeing to confinement is still seclusion (26.104).

B.q: A nurse in charge starts seclusion for Liam at 21:00. No psychiatrist authorised it. By what time should the first medical review take place?
options: By 09:00 the next day
B.why: COP15 26.116: if seclusion was authorised by the professional in charge of the ward, the RC or duty doctor should attend for the first medical review within one hour.

whyNot.0: 15 minutes is the written observation interval, not the medical review deadline.
whyNot.2: Two hours is the nursing review interval; the medical review is within one hour.
whyNot.3: Waiting until morning breaches the one-hour requirement.

B.q: Who should carry out the two-hourly nursing review of a patient in seclusion?
options: The nurse who started the seclusion, working alone
One registered nurse together with a healthcare assistant
The responsible clinician together with one nurse
Two registered nurses, one not involved in the decision
B.why: COP15 26.134: nursing reviews every two hours by two registered nurses, one of whom was not involved in the decision to seclude.

whyNot.0: A single nurse who made the decision cannot give the independent check the Code requires.
whyNot.1: The Code specifies two registered nurses.
whyNot.2: Medical reviews are separate; the nursing review is by two registered nurses.

C.q: During a restraint, Femi, 24, is held prone and gasps that he cannot breathe. His lips look dusky. What is the most appropriate immediate action by the lead nurse?
options: Keep him prone until he stops struggling
Release pressure and turn him to clear his airway
Give the prescribed IM lorazepam at once
Check his oxygen saturation after the hold ends
C.why: Restraint must not compromise airway, breathing or circulation (NG10 1.4.25; COP15 26.70-26.71). The lead protects the airway and monitors vital signs, so pressure is released and he is turned at once.

whyNot.0: Continuing prone restraint with signs of respiratory compromise risks death.
whyNot.2: Sedating someone who is struggling to breathe could worsen respiratory compromise.
whyNot.3: Monitoring is required throughout, and this is an immediate emergency.

C.q: Gina, 41, detained under section 3, has been in seclusion continuously since 07:00. It is now 15:00 and she remains very disturbed. Which review does the Code now require?
options: A second nursing review by the same two nurses
A review by the hospital managers' panel
An independent multidisciplinary review
A tribunal referral by the hospital managers
C.why: COP15 26.141: an independent MDT review is needed after 8 hours of continuous seclusion (or 12 hours intermittently within 48 hours).

whyNot.0: Two-hourly nursing reviews continue but do not replace the independent MDT review.
whyNot.1: Hospital managers' hearings concern discharge, not seclusion reviews.
whyNot.3: Tribunal referral is about detention, not the seclusion review timetable.

C.q: Two days after a restraint and rapid tranquillisation, Jordan, 29, asks why he was held. Which approach best follows NICE NG10?
options: Offer to talk it through and to record his view in his notes
Explain that incidents are discussed by staff in supervision
Tell him the incident form has already been closed
Advise him to make a formal complaint to the trust
C.why: NG10 1.4.58: give the service user the opportunity to discuss the incident in a supportive environment with staff, an advocate or carer, and offer to write their perspective in the notes.

whyNot.1: Staff discussion is separate; the patient is entitled to his own debrief.
whyNot.2: Closing a form does not meet the duty to support him to discuss the incident.
whyNot.3: He may complain, but redirecting him avoids the supportive discussion NG10 requires.

reteach.title: Airway first, safeguards always
reteach.question: What matters most in restraint and seclusion?

blocks.h: Two rules to hold on to
blocks.body: In restraint, nothing comes before airway, breathing and circulation: no pressure on neck, chest or abdomen, a lead protecting the head and neck, and the shortest possible hold. In seclusion, the legal and Code safeguards are what make it lawful: detained patients, constant sight and sound, 15-minute records, timely medical and nursing reviews, and a debrief afterwards.

items.label: first medical review if no psychiatrist

blocks.text: An informal patient who has to be secluded in an emergency needs an immediate Mental Health Act assessment.

explain.body: NG10 says avoid the floor; if needed use supine, and prone for as short a time as possible. Never restrict airway, breathing or circulation with pressure on the rib cage, neck or abdomen, or by covering the mouth or nose.

test.q: Which restraint practice does NICE NG10 prohibit?
options: Holding the arms in a standing position
Applying pressure to the rib cage
Talking to the patient during the hold
Having one staff member lead the team
test.why: NG10 1.4.25: do not restrain in a way that interferes with airway, breathing or circulation, for example by pressure on the rib cage, neck or abdomen.

whyNot.0: A standing hold avoids the floor, in line with NG10.
whyNot.3: NG10 requires a clearly defined lead.

explain.body: One staff member leads throughout. They make sure others can protect and support the head and neck, check that airway and breathing are not compromised, and monitor vital signs, and that staff are supported.

test.q: During manual restraint, what is a key responsibility of the lead staff member?
options: Completing the incident form during the hold
Holding the patient's legs securely
Protecting the head, neck and airway
Calling the police to the ward
test.why: NG10 1.4.32: the lead ensures the head and neck are protected, airway and breathing are checked and vital signs monitored.

whyNot.0: Documentation follows the incident; during it the lead protects safety.
whyNot.1: Holding limbs is another team member's role.
whyNot.3: Police involvement is not the lead's core restraint responsibility.

explain.body: Seclusion is supervised confinement away from others, for containing severe disturbance likely to harm others. It is used in hospital for detained patients. It is never punishment, a response to low staffing, or a way of managing self-harm on its own.

test.q: Which is an acceptable reason for seclusion under the MHA Code?
options: Too few staff to observe the ward
Repeated self-harm with no risk to others
Severe disturbance likely to harm others
As part of a planned behaviour programme
test.why: COP15 26.103: seclusion is for immediate necessity to contain severe behavioural disturbance likely to cause harm to others.

whyNot.1: Seclusion is not used solely to manage self-harm (26.108).
whyNot.3: Seclusion should not form part of a treatment programme (26.107).

explain.body: After restraint, rapid tranquillisation or seclusion, an immediate debrief including a nurse and a doctor looks at physical harm, ongoing risks and emotional impact. A service user-led external review follows within 72 hours.

items.label: Patient and witnesses talk it through

test.q: According to NICE NG10, by when should the formal external post-incident review take place?
options: Within 24 hours
Within 7 days
Within 28 days
Within 72 hours
test.why: NG10 1.4.62: the formal external post-incident review takes place as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after the incident.

whyNot.0: 24 hours is not the NG10 limit for the external review.
whyNot.1: 7 days is longer than NG10 allows.
whyNot.2: 28 days is far beyond the 72-hour limit.
